newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-LARA HOLDS KEY FOR WEST INDIES.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-LARA HOLDS KEY FOR WEST INDIES.

text.p: Brian Lara has set himself two goals as the West Indies begin their campaign to regain cricket supremacy against Australia -- to recapture his former glory as a batsman and steer clear of trouble.
As the world record holder for the highest score in both test and first-class cricket, Lara wants to amass enough runs to help his side recapture the Frank Worrell Trophy.
Asked about his ambitions for the coming five-test series, Lara set his sights on topping the averages, saying: "I'd like to see myself getting three centuries or even four."
But the stylish left-hander appears equally determined to avoid controversy -- a commitment that reflects the recent troubles that have blighted West Indies' cricket and his own career.
"I always wanted to keep out of trouble and I am looking forward to doing so (on this tour)," Lara told reporters after West Indies arrived in Perth on Saturday.

The tourists, who begin their preparations with a traditional tour opener against a Chairman's XI in Lilac Hill, near Perth on Monday, are faced with the unusual prospect of being regarded as underdogs going into a test series.
"I think Australia deserve to be favourites in the light of their win against us in the Caribbean 18 months ago," West Indies captain Courtney Walsh said.
Since that defeat, their first series loss in 15 years, the aura of invincibility that once surrounded West Indies cricket has faded.
At this year's World Cup, they lost to Kenya during a failed campaign that prompted the departure of captain Richie Richardson and the sackings of coach Andy Roberts and manager Wes Hall.
Lara was reportedly a central figure in the dressing room upheavals that have engulfed West Indies cricket.
Fined for indiscipline during last year's tour to England, the side's current vice-captain pulled out of a subsequent limited overs tournament in Australia. Without him, West Indies flopped badly.
On this tour, it will be the job of veteran fast bowler Walsh, coach Malcolm Marshall and tour manager Clive Lloyd to maintain team harmony.
The tourists have included rookie fast bowler Nixon McLean and promising opening batsman Adrian Griffith as the newcomers in a 16-man squad.
But much of their hopes will rest with experienced pace duo of Curtly Ambrose and Ian Bishop. In the batting ranks, Lara will be looking for support from Jimmy Adams and Shivnarine Chanderpaul.
Australia, too, have laboured a little since the euphoria of becoming the first team for more than two decades to win a test series on West Indies soil.
Last month, Mark Taylor's men lost a one-off test in India and there are reported rumblings of discontent within their ranks about the number of limited overs matches they are being asked to play.
But their major concern surrounds the condition of the most important finger in Australian sport.

Master leg-spinner Shane Warne was forced to miss the current tour to India because of an injury to the ring finger of his right hand and is battling to be fit in time for the first test in Brisbane, starting on November 22.
Warne, who is hoping to prove his recovery from finger surgery in two Sheffield Shield matches for Victoria over the coming weeks, is looking forward to his encounters with Lara.
But he played down the significance of their likely duel.
"To win a test match against West Indies you have to take 20 wickets and not just dismiss Brian Lara twice," he said.
